extracted.intended_audience: instructors and students in undergraduate discrete mathematics courses (classroom activity leaders)
extracted.subtask_description: A collection of classroom-tested discrete-mathematics activities and worksheets (topics include growth of functions/big‑O, Bulgarian Solitaire state graphs, geodesic-dome/Euler trails, and polyhedra/Euler's formula) with instructor notes, student exercises, conjectures, and worked solutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Big-Oh definition
rubrics_metrics.description: We say that a function f(x) is O(g(x)) as x tends to infinity (read “f(x) is big‑oh of g(x)”) where f and g are functions ... provided there are constants C and k such that |f(x)| ≤ C |g(x)| whenever x > k.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to talk about asymptotic growth as x→∞; small-interval behavior is not important. When using a calculator/graphing heuristic, enlarge the viewing window to see asymptotic relationships. For claims, find explicit C and k to support O(g(x)) conclusions; the worksheet asks students to graph f and g, conjecture, then produce C and k.

rubrics_metrics.name: Big‑Oh via limits (limit criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: One of the most useful characterizations of big‑oh uses limits: f(x) is O(g(x)) if lim_{x→∞} f(x)/g(x) < ∞.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To evaluate such limits typically appeal to L'Hôpital's Rule from calculus. As a heuristic you can graph the ratio f(x)/g(x) on a large window to see if it approaches a finite limit. Examples/exercises in the worksheet suggest plotting ratios to infer relationships.

rubrics_metrics.name: Little‑oh definition
rubrics_metrics.description: We say that f(x) is o(g(x)) (read f(x) is little‑oh of g(x)) if for any constant c there exists some k such that |f(x)| < c |g(x)| for x > k.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This says f grows more slowly than g and is a stronger statement than f being O(g). The worksheet suggests using a calculator to find where f(x) and c·g(x) intersect for various c (e.g., c=0.1,1,2,5,10) to find the k associated with c.

rubrics_metrics.name: Using graphing/calculator heuristics for asymptotic comparisons
rubrics_metrics.description: Graph f(x) and g(x) on windows of increasing size to get an idea whether f is O(g) (or o(g)), and to guess constants C and thresholds k.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Start with a small window to see local behavior, then enlarge the viewing window to observe long-term growth. Regraph after changing constants in front of g(x) (e.g., multiply g by C) to test conjectures. The worksheet warns that temporarily larger values for small x do not disprove asymptotic domination (e.g., 2x can be O(x^{100}) even though x^{100} > 2x for small x). Use ratio plots to supplement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparing algorithmic growth (example rubric for comparing complexities)
rubrics_metrics.description: When asked if one algorithmic complexity f(x) is O(g(x)) (e.g., merge sort x·log x vs insertion sort x^2), use definitions/limits/graphs to determine the asymptotic relationship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Graph both functions on sufficiently large windows, compute limits of ratios, or produce explicit C and k to prove O-relationships. The worksheet uses such examples to motivate the concept: merge sort ~ x·log x, insertion sort ~ x^2.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of the Bulgarian Solitaire process and cyclicity
rubrics_metrics.description: Process: from a partition of n (piles), remove one coin from each pile and form a new pile from those coins, repeat; stop when you revisit a previously encountered arrangement. An arrangement that is eventually repeated is called cyclic; the number of steps from a cyclic state to its next repeat is the cycle length; a 1‑cycle is a fixed point (unchanged by the process).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In exercises students perform the process, record progressions, and detect repeats. Instructor notes recommend demonstrating and recording states and drawing arrows to subsequent states so students see repeats; keep piles listed in increasing order for convenience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterization of fixed points (triangular states)
rubrics_metrics.description: Conjecture / result stated: A state is fixed if and only if it is of the form (k, k-1, ..., 3,2,1). There is a fixed point state for n coins iff n is a triangular number.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof sketch: show these triangle states are fixed (each pile reduced by one, eliminated smallest piles, collected pile of size k reinstates largest pile), and conversely argue that a fixed state's largest pile k forces the existence of exactly k piles of sizes k,k-1,...,1. The worksheet points to a formal reference [22].

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterization/identification of 2‑cycles
rubrics_metrics.description: Conjectured characterization: states in 2‑cycles are of specific paired forms (patterns of repeated even/odd-sized blocks); stated examples and pattern descriptions appear in the worksheet.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The worksheet notes students often guess the pattern but have difficulty proving completeness. It cites that a two‑cycle occurs exactly when the number of coins is twice a square (a result with proofs in the literature and by a student), and indicates checking that candidate forms are indeed 2‑cycles is straightforward though full classification requires more work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Garden of Eden states (no predecessor) criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: Definition: a Garden of Eden state has no predecessors (no incoming arrows). Conjecture: A state is Garden of Eden iff each pile is at least two coins smaller than the number of piles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The worksheet gives a proof sketch: if each pile is at least two less than the number of piles then any predecessor would require more coins in some pile than exist, so no predecessor exists. Conversely, if the condition fails one can construct a predecessor by taking the largest pile and distributing one coin to each of the remaining piles, creating any needed singleton piles.

rubrics_metrics.name: State graph Gn construction and drawing rules
rubrics_metrics.description: For fixed n, the state graph Gn has vertices equal to all partitions of n (arrangements); draw a directed arrow from each vertex to the vertex obtained by performing the process once. Each vertex has out‑degree one; in‑degree may be zero, one, or more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instructor advice: avoid constructing the entire graph by computing successors for all partitions at once (that tends to tangle). Instead pick a partition, draw its progression, then pick missing partitions and add their progressions, connecting as you go. Students should work on scratch paper then redraw an organized graph without crossings. Exercises include drawing G6, G7 and observing connectivity (G1–G7 connected, G8 has two components).

rubrics_metrics.name: Eulerian cycle/trail existence via vertex degrees (geodesic dome rope problem)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a graph representing pipes and joints: an Eulerian cycle (single rope passing each edge exactly once and returning to same node) exists iff every vertex has even degree. An Eulerian trail (single rope through each edge exactly once with ends at different nodes) exists iff exactly two vertices have odd degree.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply Euler's theorem: count nodes of odd degree to determine impossibility/possibility. The dome example lists six nodes of odd degree, so neither Eulerian cycle nor trail exists; hence some edges must be traversed more than once.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimizing repeated edges / minimizing rope length when >2 odd vertices
rubrics_metrics.description: If more than two odd‑degree vertices exist, choose two odd vertices to be rope ends and pair up the remaining odd vertices by duplicating (traversing twice) some edges so all other vertices become even; the minimal number of duplicate traversals corresponds to making the fewest edges doubled to achieve an Eulerian trail between chosen endpoints.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Worksheet example: with six odd nodes, choosing appropriate endpoints required traveling through four pipes twice (minimal for that dome). Guidance includes selecting which nodes should be ends, duplication choices (shorter vs longer pipes matter for total rope length), and constructing an explicit route. Practical tips: use robust rope, build from bottom up, and consider geometry (dotted shorter edges have length ratio ~0.884).

rubrics_metrics.name: Euler's formula for polyhedra / simple plane graphs
rubrics_metrics.description: Theorem (polyhedral version): Let P be any polyhedron topologically equivalent to a sphere. Let V be number of vertices, E edges, F faces. Then V − E + F = 2. The graph version: For any simple plane graph G (no loops or multiple edges), V − E + F = 2, where F includes the outside (unbounded) face.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requirements: polyhedron should be an embedded compact 2D polygonal surface with planar, nonself‑intersecting faces; simple graph assumption simplifies proofs though some versions hold more generally. Instructor notes recommend using an inductive proof on number of edges as an accessible proof in discrete math courses; activity leads students to build models, collect V,E,F and conjecture the formula.

rubrics_metrics.name: Polyhedron construction / exploration activity requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Activity directions: students build models of various polyhedra (using Polydrons or polygons cut from card stock), record V,E,F, and use collected data to conjecture Euler's formula.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical constraints: ensure polygon side lengths are equal for homemade polygons; recommended minimal counts when using homemade pieces (e.g., 76 triangles, 29 squares, 14 pentagons, 20 hexagons, 6 octagons). Instructor notes: assign different polyhedra to groups, allow early finishers to build more, and demonstrate a tetrahedron as an example; when tools are available the activity can be done in ~20 minutes, otherwise assembly increases time.
